story_text.value:
Hey HN!

I’m excited to show you my app that lets you learn any topic in a structured, bite-sized way.

Each lesson has an audio version, some visuals, and interactive quizzes. They’re personalized to your background and goals, and you can pick a concept inside a lesson and ask it to go deeper.

When my co-founder was at NotebookLM, he realized the biggest bottlenecks in learning are that people don’t have time or feel like they’re not smart enough.

We wanted to see if software can take the mental load of figuring out what resources to use and what order to learn them in, and make lessons easy to start without turning everything into just shallow summaries.

We added lots of hidden features to help you go deeper, give it a try and see if you can find some!

P.S.: My favourite feature is podcasts. They’re 3-4 mins per lesson, you can start one and it just keeps playing subsequent lessons until you stop.

I like it this way because each podcast focuses on one or two concepts and I can easily go to a specific lesson to revisit them.

Also great to listen to in the mornings when I just woke up.

Thanks for taking a look!

title.value: Show HN: Wondering – turn complex topics into short audio/visual lessons

story_text.value:
I spent 5 years working a f*cking to-do app and being a loser. Here's what I learnt.

Life planners don't work if they're too simple (e.g. Apple Notes for everything). They also don't work if they're too complicated (e.g. Notion templates).

They must be adequate, such as having basic fucking hierarchy where you can have tasks and sub-tasks. They must also be centralized, because reminders don't fucking work if I can't see them because they're hidden in 5 different places.

The resultant version is https://beta.actions.life. It's free forever for early beta users, and you can try it without going through some bullshit sign-up flow.

I hope you can tell me what's good and what's shit about the app, so I can make it better for you. Thanks.

story_text.value:
I implemented 'Restructuring Vector Quantization with the Rotation Trick' by fifty et al.and built a PyPI library for the ICLR 2025 Rotation Trick.

The Rotation Trick replaces the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) with a geometric rotation of the gradient. It preserves angular information between the encoder output and codebook vector, leading to higher codebook utilization.

I have also benchmarked it on audio. Documented everything from paper to mathematics behind in \docs in github-repo

The implementation uses matrix-free Householder reflection (O(d) memory). PyPI: pip install vqrotate Benchmark: https://github.com/develepo/vqrotate-benchmark

I also explored an adaptive scaling extension. It achieved lower MSE but introduced assignment instability, an interesting trade-off that I would love to hear thoughts on.

Would love any feedback, especially on Residual VQ extensions.

title.value: Show HN: Vqrotate – Drop-in rotation trick for VQ-VAEs

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I'm a Rwandan-American software engineer. I was fortunate enough to make it to the US, build a career here, and have opportunities that changed the trajectory of my life.

I've been thinking for a long time about how I could give something back.

So I built joinfabfriends.org.

The idea is pretty simple: think GoFundMe, but specifically for Rwandan college students who need help paying for things like tuition and textbooks.

There are incredibly talented students in Rwanda for whom a relatively small amount of money can be the difference between continuing their education and dropping out. I want Fab Friends to make that gap a little easier for people like me, and hopefully some of you to help close it.

I'm starting small. I want to learn whether this model works, how to make the process trustworthy and transparent.

And because just asking HN for money felt boring, here's my slightly unusual donor perk:

If you become a donor(Good Samaritan), you're invited to come to Rwanda with me in summer 2027.

You still have to pay your own way . I'm an engineer, not Emirates.

But I'll be your guide. We'll see Rwanda, eat very well, meet some of the students we've helped(make sure to bring hiking shoes).

I'd love your feedback, especially around:

-what level of transparency you'd expect around donations -what would make you trust/distrust a platform like this -anything about the sitethat feels confusing

And, of course, if one of the students' stories resonates with you, I'd be grateful if you became their Fab Friend.

https://joinfabfriends.org

Murakoze cyane!

story_text.value:
I built a 16-bit CPU simulator that runs entirely in the browser.

You can write assembly, run it, or step through it one instruction at a time while watching what happens inside the CPU.

It shows the registers, memory, flags, ALU, buses, and datapath as the program executes.

You can also set breakpoints, inspect execution cycles, replay previous cycles, and try some example programs.

I built this because I wanted CPU architecture to feel more tangible. Reading about fetch, decode, registers, buses, and the ALU is one thing. Watching an instruction actually move through the CPU is much more interesting.

Try it here:

https://coretrace.srianjaneyam.me/

This is my first Show HN, so I'd really appreciate feedback, especially from people interested in CPU architecture, emulators, or computer architecture education.

story_text.value:
We just released the first public results from the Agent Memory Leaderboard (AML).

The first evaluation focuses on Text Memory across two tracks:

- Open-source Methods - Commercial Products

136 teams registered, and 69 representative memory frameworks completed the first evaluation.

Commercial Products — Text Memory:

1. MemoraX — 58.02 2. MemOS — 45.89 3. NTES-MEMORY-SMART — 44.21

The benchmark uses a common evaluation framework and a clearer system boundary:

Memory system: Add → Search Benchmark: Answer → Eval

The goal is to make memory-system results more comparable and reproducible.

story_text.value:
I was always having this anxious feeling before the interview about not getting the job. Because of that, I tended to try to prep as much as I could to at least pass the first round of interview. However, interview prep research took time and was mostly the same thing: figure out what the company's dealing with, work out what the role is actually screening for, then write questions against that. When you have 2 or 3 interview invitations, you may need to spend quite some time to properly research your future employers.

This is why I built Interspectr, to automate the research and data compiling so I didn't have to do the same digging every time. Just by copy pasting the job title, company, and location from a job posting, it does online research to find the most recent company context, and generates likely questions across behavioural, technical, and company-specific categories. You can answer them and get feedback on structure. On top of that, it also suggests what questions to ask the interviewer. Finally, you can export everything to PDF/DOCX and bring it with you.

Disclaimer: the questions are predictions from the posting and public info, not reported interview questions.

Stack is React/Vite, Express, Firestore, Gemini, on Cloud Run. Free tier available, $4.99/mo beyond that. Feel free to check on the demo at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zHXSFPKBAPA.

So far it has helped 40 plus people, hoping to help more. Thanks for reading.

story_text.value:
I am generally discontent with the state of diagraming tools. They are clunky, lock you into their format and end up making unmaintainable or unintelligible diagrams.

So, I made a new tool that combines code-based diagraming with manual layout. The hope is to get the maintainability of code and the visual clarity of of hand-crafted layouts.

Give it a try and let me know your feedback. I made is as a desktop tool because there should be no reason to need to be online to use it. But I understand it limits it's accessibility. If there enough interest I may invest some time in making an online version.

So far I used it in my professional life and it saves some time and headaches.

I hope you find it interesting.

Get the release in the GitHub page or read my rant bout diagrams.

https://github.com/Sotilrac/daedalus/releases
